must_remember: In Fresnel diffraction, either the source, the screen, or both are at a finite distance from the aperture.
The wavefronts arriving at the obstacle and traveling toward the screen are spherical or cylindrical.
No lenses are required to focus the rays in Fresnel diffraction; observations are made in the near field.
The path difference from consecutive half-period zones to the observation point is $\lambda/2$, giving a phase difference of $\pi$ radians.
The resultant amplitude at an observation point is given by the alternating series $R = m_1 - m_2 + m_3 - m_4 + \dots$.
The radius of the $n$-th Fresnel zone is proportional to the square root of $n$: $r_n \propto \sqrt{n}$.
A zone plate acts like a convex lens with multiple focal lengths given by $f_n = r_1^2 / (n \lambda)$.

glossary.meaning: Diffraction phenomenon where the source or screen or both are at finite distances from the aperture, involving spherical or cylindrical wavefronts.
Concentric annular regions into which a wavefront is divided such that the path difference between consecutive zones at the observation point is $\lambda/2$.
A device constructed by alternately blocking even or odd Fresnel zones to act as a multi-focus lens.
The net optical disturbance at an observation point formed by summing the contributions from all half-period zones as $R = m_1 - m_2 + m_3 - \dots$.
